extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, policymakers, legal and environmental researchers interested in the Volkswagen 'Dieselgate' emissions scandal
extracted.subtask_description: Documenting and reporting the Volkswagen diesel-emissions scandal: events, regulatory findings, investigations, litigation, settlements, technical testing results, and industry/political reactions used for news articles or press statements about corporate regulatory breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU5 standards compliance (testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The vehicles did meet EU5 standards, so it clearly contributed to meeting the EU5 standards in testing"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: vehicles must meet EU5 emissions standards in official testing. The article documents software that altered NOx characteristics so vehicles passed EU5 lab tests while emitting more in real-world driving. Use lab vs real-world discrepancy as evidence of manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal limit for nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Real-world tests showed emissions from 37 diesel engines up to 14 times higher than had been claimed, with every vehicle exceeding the legal limit of nitrogen oxide emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: vehicles must not exceed statutory NOx limits in real-world driving. Report measured exceedances (multiples of legal limit) and sample sizes when citing non-compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of test-cycle detection software / defeat devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Only Volkswagen group vehicles were found to have test cycle detection software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: installation of software that detects test cycles or otherwise manipulates emissions testing constitutes use of a 'defeat device'. Identification of such software is central evidence of wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean Air Act violations — exceedance during normal driving and misleading omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaint alleged that Volkswagen equipped certain 2.0 and 3.0-litre diesel-engine vehicles with emissions cheating software, causing NOx pollution to exceed EPA's standards during normal driving conditions; further claimed that Volkswagen provided misleading information and that material omissions impeded efforts to learn the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal standard: liability arises if vehicles are equipped with cheating devices that cause exceedances in normal operation and if the company made misleading statements or omitted material facts. Quantify alleged damages and cite statutory penalties sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum per-vehicle civil penalty potential
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA announced that Volkswagen Group could face fines of up to US$37,500 per vehicle (about US$18 billion in total).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory penalty metric: report per-vehicle statutory maximums and aggregate potential exposure when assessing regulatory risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate penalties sought in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Justice Department complaint sought up to $46 billion in penalties for Clean Air Act violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting litigation stakes, include amounts the government seeks and distinguish between statutory maximums and amounts actually pursued or settled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall plan adequacy (performance, emissions, safety)
rubrics_metrics.description: US regulators rejected Volkswagen's recall plans for its affected 2.0-litre diesel engines, claiming that these "do not adequately address overall impacts on vehicle performance, emissions and safety".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory acceptance of recalls depends on documented effects on vehicle performance, emissions compliance in real-world driving, and safety. Rejected recall plans should be reported with regulator reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: False advertising / promotional claims accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: FTC sued Volkswagen for false advertising due to fraudulent claims made by the company in its promotion of the affected models, which touted the "environmental and economic advantages" of diesel engines and contained claims of low emissions output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising must be accurate; promotional claims about environmental performance are actionable if false or misleading. Cite specific ad claims and regulatory/alleged factual contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory orders to cease misleading advertising and devices
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. regulators such as the Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice mandated that Volkswagen cease all misleading advertising and prohibited the company from using devices intended to manipulate emission tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators can issue mandatory prohibitions and corrective orders; include scope (advertising, devices) and any compliance deadlines or monitoring obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal liability for conspiracy to defraud and obstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Volkswagen pleaded guilty to weaving a vast conspiracy to defraud the US government and obstructing a federal investigation and agreed to pay a US$2.8 billion criminal fine and US$1.5 billion in civil penalties; individuals (engineers/executives) were criminally charged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal accountability arises when evidence shows intentional design/installation of defeat devices and obstruction. Distinguish corporate pleas/penalties from individual prosecutions and include admitted facts where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer remediation options in settlement (buyback or fix, compensation amounts)
rubrics_metrics.description: About 475,000 Volkswagen owners in the US were given the choice between a buyback or a free fix and compensation, if a repair becomes available. Buybacks range in value from $12,475 to $44,176; independent of which options are selected, owners will still receive compensation ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 per affected car; leases can be terminated without penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement remedies should be reported with exact consumer options, payout ranges, and any conditions (e.g., repair availability). Note deadlines and exclusions (e.g., owners not part of class litigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental mitigation and zero-emissions infrastructure obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Volkswagen will also pay $2.7 billion for environmental mitigation and another $2 billion for clean-emissions infrastructure. The $2 billion is to be managed by Electrify America in four installments of $500 million at 2+1/2-year intervals, subject to CARB and U.S. EPA approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing corporate remediation commitments, report amounts, intended uses (mitigation vs infrastructure), implementing entities, installment schedules, and regulator approval conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on reselling repurchased vehicles unless repaired
rubrics_metrics.description: Volkswagen agreed not to resell or export any vehicles it repurchases unless an approved emission repair has been completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resale/export restrictions are common settlement safeguards to prevent circulation of non-compliant vehicles; include scope and enforcement mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing methodology reforms recommended (WLTP and PEMS / on-road testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers have criticized the inadequacy of current regulations and called for the use of a UN-sanctioned test called Worldwide harmonized Light vehicles Test Procedures that better reflects real-life driving conditions, as well as on-road emissions testing via PEMS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting on technical reform proposals should explain how WLTP and PEMS differ from lab tests (real-world conditions, portability) and note timelines/implementation status and industry lobbying/objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory investigation techniques (model sampling approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA decided to broaden its investigations onto 28 diesel-powered models ... The agency would initially focus on one used vehicle of each model, and widen the probe if it encountered suspicious data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulator investigations may use targeted sampling (one used vehicle per model) and expand based on findings. Describe sampling logic and thresholds that trigger broader probes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability exposure to state and local governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled ... that Volkswagen was liable for further legal damage lawsuits brought by state and local governments ... paved the way for counties to proceed with litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court rulings that permit state/local claims expand exposure beyond federal penalties; report jurisdictional outcomes and potential additional liabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplier potential liability (e.g., Bosch involvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The consumer settlement will resolve all claims by participating consumers against Volkswagen and all its associates, except for any potential claims against Robert Bosch GmbH. Bosch supplied two exhaust treatment components and engine control software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplier roles and contracts may create separate liability streams; identify suppliers named in suits and note exclusions in settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-impact metrics (stock price, resale value, sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Share prices fell dramatically (e.g., 20% on first trading day after EPA notice); resale values dropped 5–16% depending on model; US sales declined (23,882 vehicles in November 2015, a 24.7% decline year-over-year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify market impacts using stock movements, resale valuations, and sales figures. Provide date ranges and sources (exchange, Kelley Blue Book, sales reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical feasibility and heterogeneity of fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: VW states that Euro6 model in Germany are not affected ... 1.2 and 2.0-litre models may be updated by software, whereas the around 3 million 1.6-litre require various hardware solutions, and some cars may even be replaced. As of 28 June 2016, no practical engineering solutions that would bring the vehicles into compliance with emission standards had been publicly identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of remediation must consider model heterogeneity and whether software updates suffice or hardware replacement is required. Report engineering analyses and timelines, and note uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world compliance variability (temperature, test conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests showed compliance rates varied: a German test showed 10 out of 53 cars compliant when exposed to temperatures below 10°C; a French test showed 4 out of 52 cars compliant when tested outside; an ADAC test found 38 out of 40 diesel cars continued to fail a NOx-test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing compliance statistics, include testing conditions (ambient temperature, outside vs lab) and sample sizes. Highlight how conditions alter defeat-device behavior and emissions outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and timeliness of document production
rubrics_metrics.description: US officials criticized Volkswagen for citing German law in order to withhold documents from a group of states investigating the company's actions; Schneiderman complained over Volkswagen's slowness in producing documents from its US files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectations for corporate cooperation include timely production of relevant documents; refusals or delays citing foreign law are notable and may be criticized or legally contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative remediation proposals (promote zero-emission vehicles vs recall)
rubrics_metrics.description: An open letter urged CARB to absolve Volkswagen of recalling the 85,000 diesel vehicles affected in the US and instead allocate resources to an accelerated rollout of zero-emissions vehicles ('cure the air, not the cars'). The American Lung Association petitioned the EPA to determine Volkswagen to promote zero-emissions vehicles, build sustainable transport infrastructure and retrofit older diesel models with superior emissions controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting should lay out competing remediation proposals, their claimed emissions-reduction benefits, legal enforceability, and stakeholder support or opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate governance weaknesses as causal factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts pointed to problems in Volkswagen's corporate governance: dual-class stock gave too much power to families; government shareholding created complex decision-making; codetermination required employee representatives on the board, affecting board function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses attributing corporate misconduct to governance should identify specific governance structures and incentives, supported by expert commentary or shareholder actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescinding industry awards and reputational sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Green Car Journal rescinded its Green Car of the Year awards given to the 2009 Volkswagen Jetta TDI and 2010 Audi A3 TDI models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputational consequences include rescinded awards and de-listings from sustainability indices; report institutional actions and rationales when discussing reputational impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure commitments (charger installation specifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volkswagen planned to install hundreds of chargers with 50, 150 and even some ultra-fast 320 kW charge rate, beginning in California in 2017. Electrify America launched media campaigns and will manage $2 billion for zero-emission vehicle infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering infrastructure obligations, include technical specs (charge rates), geographic roll-out, timelines, and managing entities.
